canonical_statement: The study asked whether a structured benchmark can teach a long-horizon medical research agent while benchmark task content remains outside training.
Benchmark-as-Teacher (BaT) couples an asynchronous Stage Bank data pipeline with Bilevel Curriculum Reinforcement Learning (BiCuRL) in a recursive post-training loop.
A trained policy is termed a BaT Agent when paired with a fixed execution environment containing public stage skills; this engineering layer is held fixed across BaT Agent comparisons.
Stage Bank exposes three content-isolated training pools: S-target for the selected weak stage, S-mix for remaining stages, and an E2E surrogate for complete-workflow coordination.
AutoMedBench-Lite supplies five public workflow stages—Plan, Setup, Validate, Inference, and Submit—each with a stage score and rubric.
The Data Factory asks teacher models to generate fictional medical-imaging tasks and complete them as multi-turn trajectories outside the policy-update loop.
A leakage preflight rejects held-out identifiers, paths, reports, traces, answers, and evaluation-derived metadata before a Stage Bank row enters training.
Aggregate recording statistics may guide Stage Bank synthesis, but raw evaluation content is not inserted into Stage Bank prompts or rows.
SFT rows retain multi-turn task history and tool observations as context but apply loss only to one selected teacher response.
RL rows are executable sandboxes reconstructed at a public stage boundary with files, tools, intermediate artifacts, a stage goal, execution procedure, recovery steps, and rubric.
Each verified Stage Bank row stores sandbox state, stage/E2E label, rubric items, evidence requirements, stage skill, and provenance, with a stable state_id linking rollouts from the row.
BiCuRL alternates finite GRPO training blocks with controller evaluation, curriculum updates, and checkpoint retention.
Controller evaluation and final evaluation use disjoint runs; only five stage scores and one Overall score leave controller evaluation, and controller rollouts are discarded.
In the BiCuRL inner loop, an LLM verifier scores rollouts against rubric items using execution records and artifact evidence and reports evidence completeness.
The outer curriculum selects the weak stage from fixed held-out stage diagnostics and mixes targeted-stage, other-stage, and E2E sandboxes for the next round.
Checkpoint fallback is triggered after three consecutive controller score drops or when KL divergence exceeds 0.1.
Stage Bank contained 20,299 candidate prompt states and a synthetic E2E source pool of 1,008 rows.

population.label: Stage Bank candidate prompt states and E2E source rows

canonical_statement: The SFT cold start for each 4B and 9B model used 4,608 training rows with no evaluation rows.
The Qwen3.5-9B SFT cold start used full-parameter training on 8 GPUs with FSDP, global batch size 64, learning rate 2e-5, 200 steps, and seed 42.
The recorded serving setup used 8 NVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs, default SGLang serving, a 256K context, and reported descriptive throughput of 320 tokens/s for 4B and 220 tokens/s for 9B.
AutoMedBench-Lite Overall is the mean of Task and Agentic scores; Agentic combines Plan, Setup, Validate, Inference, and Submit with weights 0.25, 0.15, 0.35, 0.15, and 0.10.

outcome.definition: Mean of Task and Agentic; Agentic weighted stage score

canonical_statement: AutoMedBench-Lite evaluation uses seven tracks with 10 repeats per track, yielding 70 runs per system; the statistical unit is the track.

The matched Qwen3.5-9B pool-ablation contract used minibatch 8, four rollouts per prompt, actor learning rate 1e-6, KL coefficient 1e-3, temperature 0.7, 10 rounds of 50 steps, optimizer reset between rounds, and 7 tracks × 10 repeats for final evaluation.
Across SFT stage/E2E rows, each stored row was a single-response slice (1.0 turn) and each stage stored about 2.0K rows.

canonical_statement: AutoMedBench-Lite participates in adaptation through aggregate diagnostic signals, so it cannot be treated as an untouched final test even though task content is kept outside training rows.
A separate untouched final test and a measured semantic-leakage audit remain future work.
The external-benchmark table combines retained local runs with published baselines, and the local aggregates lack complete per-run manifests.
BaT-4B underperformed its baseline on all eight external benchmarks, while BaT-9B improved on only three of five long-horizon external tasks.
Top-tier comparisons evaluate complete agent systems with their named execution settings and therefore support only system-level, not policy-isolated, claims.

The Limitations subsection states that the evidence has six limits but enumerates only four numbered items before the paper transitions to Related Work; two asserted limits are not identifiable from the source text.
The authors conclude that a structured benchmark can act as both evaluator and post-training teacher through Stage Bank, BiCuRL, and a fixed agent execution layer.
The authors conclude that BaT-9B largely retained short-turn reasoning and improved three of five long-horizon external scores, whereas BaT-4B showed broad external regressions.
The paper reports public release of the BaT code at the AutoMedBench/Benchmark-as-Teacher GitHub repository.
